text: , dipyridamole, given alone or with aspirin, is effective for secondary prevention,42 but use of clopidogrel with aspirin increases the risk of bleed- ing without reducing the risk of ischaemic events.43 Clopi- dogrel with aspirin is of benefit in patients with acute cor- onary syndromes, but in patients with high cardiovascular risk who do not present acutely the increased bleeding risk appears to outweigh any benefit.44 Oral anticoagulants may be more effective than antiplatelet therapy but the risk of bleeding is increased,31,45 and they are generally only recommended in patients unable to take antiplatelet drugs or in whom they are ineffective. Addition of antiplatelet drugs in patients taking oral anticoagulants for other indi- cations only appears to be beneficial in those with mechan- ical heart valves.46 Lipid lowering therapy has an established role in cardio- vascular risk reduction, and the benefits of statins, in par- ticular, have been demonstrated in a wide range of pa- tients. Meta-analyses47-52 have shown that statins improve outcomes when used for primary or secondary prevention, and that this includes patients with raised or average cho- lesterol concentrations, women, and older individuals. The absolute benefit depends on the patient’s initial cardiovas- cular risk and the degree of cholesterol reduction achieved,51 and increased benefit has been reported53-55 with the use of intensive lipid lowering regimens. Al- though most recent studies have used statins, fibrates56 and other lipid lowering drugs may also be effective; beneficial effects for secondary prevention of ischaemic heart dis- ease have been reported for gemfibrozil57 in men whose primary lipid abnormality was a low HDL-cholesterol lev- el, and for omega-3 marine triglycerides58 in a Mediterra- nean population. There has been concern that there might be an association between low cholesterol concentrations and increased morbidity and mortality from non-cardiac causes includ- ing haemorrhagic stroke, cancer, accidents and suicide, and chronic respiratory, liver, and bowel disease.59-64 Al- though controlled studies suggest that the risk of haemorr- hagic stroke may be increased,65 meta-analyses have shown that statin therapy reduces both cardiovascular and all-cause mortality,47,50,51 and that there is no significant increase in non-illness mortality.66 The use of ACE inhibitors has mainly been investigated in individuals with established cardiovascular disease. Studies67,68 in patients with heart failure suggested that ACE inhibitors also reduced the risk of myocardial infarc- tion, while in the HOPE study,69 treatment with ramipril significantly reduced the rate of death, myocardial infarc- tion, and stroke in patients at high risk for cardiovascular disease.
